children: Sun Pharmaceutical Industries has agreed to extend "most favoured nation" (MFN) drug pricing to US state Medicaid programmes and future innovative medicine launches in exchange for a delay in impending American tariffs, India's largest drugmaker said on September 1.
The announcement came during a White House signing ceremony attended by several pharmaceutical manufacturers.
Because most details of the agreement remain confidential, the immediate financial impact on the drugmaker is difficult to quantify.

"We are proud to play our part in delivering the medicines that millions of American patients count on every day," said Rick Ascroft, North America CEO of Sun Pharma, who represented the company at the White House ceremony.
Sun Pharma said the agreement recognises company's investment in the US market by delaying Section 232 tariffs on innovative pharmaceutical products for over two years.
MFN pricing involves a pharmaceutical company voluntarily agreeing to sell a drug to US government health programmes at comparable pricing in another advanced market.

US President Donald Trump has threatened 100 percent tariff on imported branded pharmaceutical products and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), arguing that Americans pay far more for medicines than patients in other developed countries.
The agreement comes as Trump administration seeks to bring down prescription drug costs while simultaneously encouraging pharmaceutical investment in America.
While previous attempts to impose MFN pricing through regulation faced legal and political hurdles, the White House now appears to be pursuing voluntary agreements with manufacturers.
For Sun Pharma, the US is, too, important to ignore.
The company said the US generates roughly 27 percent of its global revenue and is its largest market for innovative medicines.

Over the past decade, Sun Pharma has evolved from being primarily a generic-drug supplier into a specialty pharmaceutical company with growing franchises in dermatology, immunology, ophthalmology and oncology.
The agreement's most notable benefit for the company is the delay of potential Section 232 tariffs on innovative pharmaceutical products for more than two years.

Section 232 refers to a US national security provision that can be used to impose tariffs on imported goods, including medicines. Such tariffs have been a major concern for the pharmaceutical industry because of their potential to disrupt supply chains and increase costs.
For Sun Pharma, avoiding tariffs may be worth more than the near-term revenue impact of extending MFN pricing, especially given its ambitions to deepen its US footprint.

The timing is notable. Earlier this year, Sun Pharma announced a definitive agreement to acquire Organon & Co in a deal valued at $11.75 billion, one of the largest acquisitions in the company's history.
The transaction underscores Sun Pharma's desire to expand its presence in the US healthcare market and build greater scale in branded medicines.

Against that backdrop, the White House agreement allows Sun Pharma to position itself as a cooperative partner in the administration's affordability agenda while safeguarding a market that is central to its future growth.

title: Sun Pharma signs US drug pricing deal, secures tariff relief for 2 years
